preamble: Voicing of the postalveolar fricative [ʃ] to [ʒ] comes from regressive voicing assimilation before a voiced consonant, within words and across word boundaries. Hungarian applies it to all obstruent clusters, so s /ʃ/ becomes [ʒ] before a voiced obstruent (hasba [ˈhɒʒbɒ]). In European and Carioca Portuguese the postalveolar coda sibilant is [ʃ] before voiceless sounds and pause but [ʒ] before voiced consonants, and Catalan final x /ʃ/ is voiced before a voiced consonant in the next word (peix gran [ˈpeʒ‿ˈɣɾan]).

examples.note: Regressive voicing assimilation: all obstruents in a cluster take the voicing of the last one, also across word boundaries (cf. the reverse rúzstól [ˈruːʃtoːl] 'from lipstick').

examples.from: coda sibilant [ʃ] (as before voiceless consonants, e.g. festa [ˈfɛʃtɐ] 'party')
examples.note: The postalveolar coda sibilant of European (and Carioca) Portuguese is voiced to [ʒ] before a voiced consonant; Brazilian varieties outside Rio have alveolar /ˈmez.mu/.
Across a word boundary the final sibilant becomes voiced before a word beginning with a voiced consonant.
Obstruents assimilate to the voicing of a following voiced consonant or vowel, also across word boundaries.

context: Before a voiced obstruent (Hungarian, Portuguese) or a voiced consonant or vowel in the next word (Catalan)
allophones_note: /ʃ/ (or the coda sibilant) surfaces as [ʒ] before voiced sounds and stays [ʃ] before voiceless sounds and pause.
